phonemes.desc: Alpha with acute pitch [á] — a bright, open attack; the whole name flashes on its first syllable.
Rolled alveolar rho [r] — the quick turn at the name's center.
Voiced velar gamma with short omicron and final sigma [gos] — clipped, unlenited, watchful.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AR-goss' — two short syllables, stress forward, like a light snapping on.

kin.label: Greek adjective
kin.form: ἀργός, 'shining, white, gleaming' — and, by the flash of motion, 'swift'

kin.label: Epithet
kin.form: Πανόπτης (Panoptēs), 'the All-Seeing', his fixed title in the myth

pronunciation.note: Árgos is Tier 2 because the Greek Ἄργος carries only the acute stress; both vowels are short, so a single feature separates the restoration from ASCII. The name belongs to the giant Argos Panoptes, Hera's watcher — not to the city of the Argolid, though the two share the shining root.

domains.title: The All-Seeing Watcher
domains.subtitle: Vigilance, Service, and the Hundred Eyes
domains.lead: Árgos Panoptes is the perfect sentinel of Greek myth: a giant whose body was set with eyes that slept only in relays, so that some were always open. Hera chose him to guard the cow that had been Io. He is the myth's meditation on watchfulness — its power, its cost, and its strange afterlife in feathers.

cards.name: The Hundred Eyes
cards.desc: Ovid gives him a hundred eyes ringed about his head; the tragedians make him many-eyed, and later art covers his whole body with them. Two slept while the others watched.

cards.name: Hera's Guard
cards.desc: Chosen by the queen of heaven herself to watch Io — the one servant whose vigilance could be trusted absolutely.

cards.name: The Sleepless Watch
cards.desc: His eyes took turns at rest; there was no hour, no dusk, no dawn in which the prisoner was unseen.

cards.name: The Peacock's Tail
cards.desc: Slain by Hermês, he was memorialized by his mistress: Hera set his eyes on the tail of her bird, where they watch still.

symbols.name: The peacock
symbols.meaning: Hera's bird; the eyes on its tail are his memorial

symbols.name: The white cow
symbols.meaning: Io transformed, the charge he was set to guard

symbols.name: The herdsman's staff
symbols.meaning: His gear as a common cowherd on the roads of the Argolid

symbols.name: The curved sword
symbols.meaning: The harpē of Hermês, by which the watcher was finally put to sleep

mythology.lead: Árgos exists within a single great story — the wanderings of Io — but it is one of the oldest stories the Greeks told, already old when Homer gave Hermês the epithet Argeiphontēs, 'Slayer of Árgos' (Iliad 24.24). His myths are few because his function is single: he is watchfulness, given a hundred eyes and a herd.

myths.title: Hera Sets the Watch
myths.text: Zeús pursued Io, daughter of the river-god Inachos, and — in the common telling — Hera's jealousy had the girl changed into a white cow, either by the goddess herself or by Zeús trying to hide the affair (Aeschylus, Suppliants 291–324; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.588–600). Hera was not deceived. She took the cow as a gift and set over it the giant Árgos Panoptes, the All-Seeing, whose body — Ovid gives him a hundred eyes — slept in relays so that some were always open (Met. 1.625–630). He tethered his charge to an olive tree in the grove of Mycenae and watched her day and night: a princess grazing as a beast, guarded by a creature made of vigilance (Apollodorus 2.1.3). The myth sets its terms without mercy: Io's misery is total, Árgos's attention is total, and between the two there is no gap anywhere for pity to enter. The story begins by defining a perfect system — and spends the rest of its time finding the one flaw a system cannot see.

myths.title: The Herdsman Who Never Sleeps
myths.text: Árgos kept Io as a cowherd keeps a beast: by day she grazed under his eyes, by night she was bound to her tree (Apollodorus 2.1.3). The poets dwell on the horror of the arrangement — Aeschylus stages the tormented cow as a speaking suppliant in the Suppliants, while Ovid lingers over the hundred eyes that closed only two at a time, like lamps going out in sequence across a darkened house (Metamorphoses 1.625–630). Notably, the myth does not make Árgos cruel. He is simply, absolutely, employed: duty incarnate, a mind with no interior, no sleep, no dream, whose only relation to the world is the unbroken line of his gaze. That purity of function is what makes him mythic rather than monstrous — and what makes his eventual death feel less like the slaying of a villain than the unplugging of an instrument. Watchfulness itself, the myth observes, is neither good nor evil; it is only total — and totality is what finally draws the god's sword.

myths.title: Hermês Argeiphontēs
myths.text: Zeús could not free Io by force without open war upon Hera, so he sent Hermês to end the watch by craft (Homeric Hymn to Hermes knows the god as thief and trickster from birth). Disguised as a shepherd, the god played his pipes to the giant — and Ovid makes his true soporific instrument the story itself: he tells the tale of Syrinx, the nymph who fled Pan's pursuit and became the singing reeds, and one by one the hundred eyes grow heavy and close (Metamorphoses 1.668–721). Then Hermês draws the curved sword and strikes off the watcher's head. The epithet that clings to the god forever after — Argeiphontēs, Slayer of Árgos — is already alive in Homer, which proves the story's antiquity: the Iliad can use the title without explanation, as a name the audience would recognize at once (Iliad 24.24). It is the most civilized killing in Greek myth, and the most ominous. The watcher who saw everything was not overpowered; he was sung to sleep — the oldest recorded defeat of total vigilance by art.

myths.title: The Eyes on the Peacock
myths.text: Hera took the eyes of her dead servant and set them in the tail of her peacock, where they gleam like jewels to this day (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.722–723). But she did not forgive the prisoner: she sent a gadfly to sting Io into madness and drive her over the world — past the Bosporos, the cow-ford that still bears her name, down to Egypt, where Zeús restored her with a touch and she bore Epaphos (Aeschylus, Suppliants; Apollodorus 2.1.3–4). The memorial is the myth's most beautiful and most ambivalent image. The goddess honors her servant's vigilance by preserving his eyes — yet the eyes now watch nothing at all: gorgeous, useless, fixed on no one, a constellation of attention without an object. Árgos's whole life is compressed into ornament. Total attention is honored by its owner, rewarded with beauty, and ended by a story — and the peacock's tail remains the most gorgeous surveillance apparatus in the world, watching nothing whatsoever.

lore.syncretism: Árgos never became a god and was never identified with foreign deities; his afterlife is in the natural world and in language. Rome kept him as Argus — Ovid's account in the Metamorphoses is the fullest surviving version — and made the transfer of his eyes the aition, the explanatory myth, of the peacock's plumage. Later readers saw in his hundred eyes the starry sky itself, set as heaven's watchman over the world. His name also lives disguised in Hermês's oldest epithet: Argeiphontēs appears already in the Iliad, proof that the story of the slain watcher was archaic before Homer sang.
lore.culturalLegacy: English keeps him in the phrase 'argus-eyed', watchful beyond fatigue. Newspapers across the English-speaking world took the name The Argus — the all-seeing press — and naturalists gave it to the argus pheasant, whose feathers are spotted with eyes in exact obedience to the myth. Every camera grid and sensor network re-enacts him: Árgos is the mythic ancestor of all surveillance, and his fate is its parable. The watcher who saw everything was undone by music and a story — the oldest recorded defeat of total vigilance by art. In the Argolid itself, his name still colors the landscape: the citadel of Árgos and the Heraion, sanctuary of his mistress, keep the shining root that named both the giant and the city.
lore.extendedMeditation:
There is a peculiar pathos in Árgos. He is the one figure in the Io story without desire: Zeús wants, Hera rages, Io suffers, but Árgos only watches. He is duty itself, a creature made of attention. The myth does not call him wicked; Hera's grief for him is real, and his memorial is beautiful. Yet the story knows that perfect vigilance is a kind of death-in-life — a mind with no interior, no sleep, no dream.

And so the manner of his fall matters. He is not overpowered; no hero wrestles him down. He is lulled — by music, and by a story about the music. The hundred eyes close one after another, like lamps in a city at midnight, and in the last of them the sword is already falling. It is the most civilized killing in Greek myth, and the most ominous: attention can be sung to sleep. Hera could preserve his eyes, but not his seeing. The peacock's tail is the most gorgeous surveillance apparatus in the world, and it watches nothing at all.
lore.archaeology: Árgos Panoptes had no cult and no temple; the Greeks themselves knew him as a figure of the primeval Argolid, and his material presence is pictorial. Attic and South Italian vases of the fifth and fourth centuries BCE show him exactly as the poets describe — a herdsman whose body is seeded with eyes, standing guard over the cow Io, or falling beneath Hermês's sword. His landscape survives: the Heraion of Argos, the great sanctuary of his mistress, and the olive grove of Mycenae where the sources place his watch. The myth's honesty is part of its interest — the all-seeing watcher left nothing behind but pictures of his own watching.
